Spinner · the network round

Round one was four ways to spin a ring, and you were right that none of them said anything. These four say something specific: D3 draws force-directed graphs and the cloud is the link, so the spinner is a small network with something moving through it rather than a wheel going round.

Same rules as before — live, at 14, 16, 20 and 24px, on the page ground and inside a primary button, with the reduced-motion version beside it. Judge them at 14px: a three-node graph has more to lose at that size than a ring does.

E · Relay

Three nodes in a ring, and a signal hopping edge to edge — each hop wakes the node it arrives at. The most literal reading of a network: this is a graph, and something is moving through it.

F · Packets

Data travelling a link, drawn as dots marching around it. Same footprint as the spinner it replaces, so it is the most legible of the four at 14px — the ring is doing the work, and the packets are the detail.

G · Uplink

One node reaching another, over and over: a hub, an arm sweeping around it, and a satellite that dims as it goes away and brightens as it comes back. Client and cloud, which is the other half of the name.

H · Mesh

A force graph settling and unsettling — the triangle contracts and rotates as if a simulation were still resolving, nodes pulsing out of phase. The closest to what D3 actually draws.

The honest risk with this direction. A ring is legible at 14px because it is one shape. A graph is three nodes and three edges, and at 14px each node is about 3px across with a 1px edge between them — which is why Packets keeps the ring and spends the detail on what travels along it, and why Relay and Mesh are the two to look at hardest in the small column before choosing either.
